section_summary: This section covers the implementation of Japan’s Nine Point Economic Stabilization Program and the Economic Stabilization Board’s response to the Dodge budget. SCAP memoranda report measures on public finance, taxation, credit, wages, trade, rationing, production, and food collection. A later Board study argues that rapid stabilization could restrict investment, reduce production, and cause extensive unemployment.

subfiles.title: Economic Stabilization Board memorandum on Japan’s economic situation, concluding page
subfiles.about: Argues that Japan must save, expand exports, and accumulate capital to become self-supporting.
subfiles.summary: Concludes that Japanese living standards must remain constrained while production supports investment and exports.

subfiles.title: Implementation of the Nine Point Economic Stabilization Program in Japan
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits SCAP memoranda on implementation and progress of the stabilization program.
subfiles.summary: Reviews the December 1948 directive and Japan’s response, introduces three enclosed memoranda, and reports that the mission will provide periodic updates.

subfiles.title: Program to Achieve Economic Stabilization in Japan Pursuant to Interim Directive of the United States Government
subfiles.about: Sets out measures to implement each objective of the Nine Point Program.
subfiles.summary: The program calls for balanced budgets, stronger tax enforcement, restricted credit, wage and price stability, and tighter foreign exchange controls. It also details rationing, material allocation, production, agricultural, and fisheries measures intended to expand exports and improve food collection.

subfiles.title: Progress Report on Program to Achieve Economic Stabilization
subfiles.about: Records actions taken after the December 1948 economic stabilization directive.
subfiles.summary: Lists developments in trade, government staffing, tax prosecutions, bank lending, wage negotiations, price controls, foreign exchange, rationing, industrial production, and food collection through early February 1949.

subfiles.title: Progress Report on Program to Achieve Economic Stabilization
subfiles.about: Updates the February report on implementation of the Nine Point Program.
subfiles.summary: Reports a balanced budget proposal, tax evasion prosecutions, limits on Reconstruction Finance Bank borrowing, wage restraint, revised trade controls, textile allocations, coal policy, and added electric power and shipbuilding.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-96 on Japanese economic and trade developments
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports disputes and negotiations concerning Japan’s rehabilitation, trade, and tax policy.
subfiles.summary: Discusses Colonel Pope’s reported criticism of SCAP, Chinese equipment offered for sale, prospective trade arrangements, Korean and Mexican trade, a tax study, and concern over tax collection. Page 376 has no readable OCR.

subfiles.title: Airgram from Tokyo, largely illegible
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: A separate incoming airgram survives in OCR with its substantive text largely unreadable.
subfiles.summary: The header suggests a Tokyo airgram dated April 28, 1949; its subject and contents cannot be reliably recovered.

subfiles.title: Economic Stabilization Board’s Reactions to Nine Point Program and Dodge Budget
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits and analyzes two Economic Stabilization Board memoranda.
subfiles.summary: Sebald explains the Board’s preference for gradual stabilization and continued investment, contrasting it with Dodge’s balanced budget and credit restrictions. He notes the Board’s fears of deflation, reduced production, and a tight money market, and calls for careful supervision of public finance.

subfiles.title: Stabilization and Reconstruction
subfiles.about: Argues for gradual stabilization accompanied by capital accumulation and investment.
subfiles.summary: The Board contrasts its staged approach with rapid currency and budget stabilization, arguing that restricted credit would reduce industrial funds and purchasing power. It forecasts production shortfalls, business failures, and unemployment, then examines likely damage to agriculture, public works, transport, and electric power. Its conclusion urges gradual disinflation, revised prices, selective investment, and use of foreign trade surplus funds for long-term development.
